Hi Simon, thanks for covering skill-placebo, it's a genuinely interesting study. But I would push back on "some of the most popular skills ... are now basically useless". Having dug into the published logs and re-run part of it myself, I think that's a shortcut:

First, the benchmark runs short tasks with a fully autonomous agent: no human in the loop, no grilling, no specs, no planning, no back-and-forth with the user. That interaction is exactly where plugins like mattpocock/skills shine, and 14 of its 25 skills are user-only by design (disable-model-invocation: true). That includes implement, the skill that drives Matt's whole implementation workflow: TDD at pre-agreed seams, then a code-review pass. And TDD itself requires confirming the seams with the user before writing any test, which is impossible in an unattended run. In the published logs, the agent never invoked a single mattpocock skill: 0 of 30 runs.

Second, the benchmark only checks whether hidden tests pass. Some skills target code quality and maintainability, like Karpathy's simplicity and surgical changes, or ponytail's "write less code". The benchmark doesn't measure that: a clean fix and a messy one score the same. Even so, ponytail was the one pack with a clear measurable effect: about 12% lower cost than the placebo.

Third, skills like caveman or i-have-adhd mainly shape the style of the replies. Some people simply prefer short, structured answers, and that's a matter of taste, not of passing tests.

Finally, I re-ran the benchmark locally with mattpocock/skills (90 trials). The success rate came out at 97% with the skills, against 83% with the placebo and 87% with no skill. The study found the opposite (83% vs 87% placebo). And again, the skills were never invoked (0 of 30)! Same benchmark, same model, opposite result: the pass-rate numbers are quite noisy.

So, "basically useless" doesn't seem a fair reading of the study. Would be curious to hear your take.

That advisor setup is unnecessary. I'm using a workflow with an opus 5.5/high orchestrator, and a variety of permanent subagent. The workflow was based on extensive benchmarking of Sonnet 5.5 for coding - on low, medium, and high effort. It used a developed set of subagents, specialized for specific tasks like reviewing all code, testing (and developing tests for) the code, sending rework back to the writing agent, and cycling all that until either refutation and final acceptance agents have no objections, or a fixed number of turns was reached, at which point it took the best result up to that point. All these managing agents were automatically assigned a model and effort level by the orchestrator. Some are Opus, usually high or medium effort, some are Sonnet, usually low or medium effot.

And finally - similar to your advisor case - in those examples when the rework cycles run out, and it has the best effort, it then gives a Fable agent a crack on solving it. All I had to do to set that up was tell the orchestrator to do just that. And it worked, with Fable taking an incredibly tough, real world code design problem from that huge legacy codebase project that had run out of solutions without a completely satisfactory one, and in about 2 minutes understanding the entire design intent, solving the problem with real code. But the framework still ran it through refutation, code check, live testing, and everything that failed the prior attempts, and the solution was a pass. Two minutes, on a problem that stumped a team of well trained, cooperating agents, which had been performing flawlessly on project tasks up to that time. In fact, it was having the team hit that wall that resulted in me adding the "Master Coding Agent" into the workflow, invoked only on those tasks where it runs out of any acceptable solutions.
